summary.text: The First Crusade (1096–1099) was the first of a series of religious wars initiated, supported and at times directed by the Latin Church in the Middle Ages.
It began in 1095 when Byzantine emperor Alexios I asked for military support, and Pope Urban II then urged faithful Christians to make an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem.
The crusaders stormed and captured Jerusalem on 15 July 1099, and four Crusader states were established in the Holy Land.

facts.label: End of the crusade
facts.value: A Fatimid counterattack was repulsed at Ascalon

items.prompt: In 1095 an emperor in Constantinople sent ambassadors asking for military help against Seljuk-led Turks. What did the pope do soon after?

options.label: He refused and told Christians to avoid war
He backed the plea and urged an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem
He ordered the emperor to send envoys to Rome
He sent a legation to excommunicate the emperor

items.explain: At the Council of Clermont, Pope Urban II gave a speech supporting the Byzantine request and urging faithful Christians to undertake an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

items.prompt: A band of poor Christians led by a French priest sets off before the nobles' armies. What awaits them in Anatolia?

options.label: A Turkish ambush that wipes them out
A quick victory at the gates of Nicaea
A safe march under Byzantine protection
A peace treaty with the Seljuk ruler

items.explain: The poor Christians led by Peter the Hermit were annihilated in a Turkish ambush at the Battle of Civetot after leaving Byzantine-controlled territory in Anatolia.

items.prompt: A theologian says a war can be justified if a legitimate authority such as a king or bishop proclaims it, it is defensive or recovers lands, and it avoids excessive violence. Which war fits?

options.label: One launched by any warlord to seize new territory
One proclaimed by a king solely to raise plunder
One begun without any authority to punish a rival
One proclaimed by a bishop to recover lost lands without excessive violence

items.explain: Augustine wrote that aggressive war was sinful, but war could be justified if a legitimate authority proclaimed it, it was defensive or for recovering lands, and it avoided excessive violence.

items.prompt: In the 11th century the Byzantines needed military help. Why did that find a ready audience among Western warriors?

options.label: The warrior class had lost trust in the pope
The warrior class wanted to avoid fighting each other
The western warrior class had become more willing to accept papal military command
The warrior class had been ordered home by the Byzantines

items.explain: The Byzantine need for military support coincided with an increase in the willingness of the western European warrior class to accept papal military command.

items.prompt: Jerusalem has fallen to the crusaders, but the Fatimids strike back later in 1099. How does that end?

items.explain: A Fatimid counterattack was repulsed later that year at the Battle of Ascalon, which marked the end of the First Crusade.

items.prompt: By the 11th century Jerusalem had been Muslim-ruled for hundreds of years. What newly began to threaten local Christians, pilgrimages and the Byzantine Empire?

options.label: A ban on pilgrimage by the Eastern church
The practices of the Seljuk rulers in the region
The westward spread of the Reconquista
Pope Leo IX's break with Constantinople

items.explain: Although Jerusalem had been ruled by Muslims for hundreds of years, the practices of the Seljuk rulers began to threaten local Christians, pilgrimages and the Byzantine Empire.

paragraphs.heading: What it was
paragraphs.text: The First Crusade, fought from 1096 to 1099, was the first in a series of religious wars started, backed and sometimes led by the Latin Church in the Middle Ages. Their goal was to put the Holy Land back under Christian rule, centuries after the Rashidun Caliphate had conquered it in the 7th century. It ended with Jerusalem in crusader hands and four Crusader states founded in the region.

paragraphs.heading: A call for help
paragraphs.text: In the 11th century, how the Seljuks ruled the area started to endanger local Christians, Western pilgrims and the Byzantine Empire itself. In 1095 the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos sent envoys to the Council of Piacenza asking for military help against the Seljuk-led Turks. Later that year, at the Council of Clermont, Pope Urban II backed the request. He urged Christians to set out on an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

paragraphs.heading: The People's Crusade
paragraphs.text: People of every social class in western Europe answered the call with enthusiasm. The first to march were thousands of mostly poor Christians led by a French priest, Peter the Hermit. On their way through Germany they attacked Jews, including in the Rhineland massacres. Once they left Byzantine lands in Anatolia, a Turkish force under Kilij Arslan I ambushed and destroyed them at Civetot in October 1096.

paragraphs.heading: The Princes' Crusade
paragraphs.text: Great nobles and their followers set out in late summer 1096 and reached Constantinople over the following months. Counting non-fighters, their forces may have reached 100,000 people. In Anatolia they won at the Siege of Nicaea in June 1097, helped by a Byzantine attack from the water, and beat Turkish mounted archers at Dorylaeum in July. After a hard march they besieged Antioch and took it in June 1098.

paragraphs.heading: Jerusalem and after
paragraphs.text: The crusaders reached Jerusalem, then held by the Fatimids, in June 1099. They stormed it on 15 July 1099 and massacred a large share of its people. A Fatimid counterattack was beaten off at Ascalon later that year, which closed the crusade, and most crusaders then went home. The Crusaders kept some foothold in the region until Acre, their last major stronghold, fell in 1291.

paragraphs.heading: Why Europe was ready
paragraphs.text: Europe's population had grown a great deal by the 11th century, and the Catholic Church had become a dominant force. Western society ran on feudalism, a system in which knights and nobles owed military service to their lords in exchange for income from land. The Byzantine plea for help came just as Western warriors were growing more willing to take military orders from the pope. A Christian idea of holy war went back to the 4th-century theologian Augustine of Hippo. He called aggressive war a sin, but allowed war declared by a proper authority, fought in defence or to recover land, and free of excessive violence.
